voice_attribution_risks.note: several economists' contradictory claims are summarised in one sentence without quote marks; the irony needs care
Burke's claim about five labourers is given in the footnote; the 'sophist and sycophant' label is Marx's own voice
the Spectator's view on the Rochdale experiment and Comte's 'eternal necessity' are quoted or ironic; not Marx's claims
Adam Smith's view that the difference is 'merely subjective' is stated before Marx answers it
Garnier's argument against educating workers is set in quotation with no tag until after; irony must be carried by the wording alone
Plato's and Xenophon's views on specialisation are stated as theirs; the 'bourgeois instinct' and Platonisme jibes are Marx's
a string of rival definitions of machine (mathematicians, Schulz) before Marx rejects them
Mill's question is an opponent's view; footnote 1 is Marx's sarcastic correction
Ure's blame of 'self-willed' workers is a quote; the mockery is Marx's
the Urquhart quote and Hegel footnote read as opinions Marx is cataloguing, not endorsing

irony_examples.note: economists praise labour's gratitude to capital, then demand 15-hour days; Marx mocks their inconsistency
Burke called 'sophist and sycophant' for claiming five farm labourers are interchangeable
footnote 7: Aristotle's social animal is set beside Franklin's tool-making animal as 'characteristic of Yankeedom'
footnote 15: 'That Philistine paper' and 'Quelle horreur!' mock the Spectator's fear of masters being pushed out
footnote 18: Comte's school made feudal lords 'an eternal necessity' as with capitalist lords
footnote 35: Yankee tax on umbrella parts, an 'assemblage of taxes'
'the enthusiastic apologists of the factory system' decry a plan of society as 'one immense factory'
Garnier 'quite naturally' rose to senator, 'quite as naturally' opposing education; 'homeopathic doses' of Smith's proposal
Roscher's 'Jovian head' and 'various wages' mock the idea that the capitalist invents division of labour
'friend Ure' and the 'infirmity of human nature' quote: the self-willed worker is blamed for resisting
footnote 7: the 'Christian philanthropists of Germany' who put boards on serfs' necks to stop them eating flour
'Thor' hyperbole about a steam hammer that could not be wielded by the god
